title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This cabinet was built for the Grateful Dead’s 1974 Wall of Sound and originally housed a speaker that carried Phil Lesh’s bass or piano. In 1991, the cabinet was acquired by Simon Babbs, son of Ken Babbs who was a member of the Merry Pranksters and close collaborator of founder Ken Kesey. The cabinet was moved to the Kesey farm in Oregon where it was highly modified and painted red and white and then actively used by the Merry Pranksters Band. Photographs from early 1990s Fourth of July parties show the red Wall of Sound derived cabinets on the back of Kesey’s stage truck, with Ken and his wife Faye performing in front of them.  Cabinet has various stickers affixed including BOAC (British Airways) for air cargo for the 1974 European tour. Hand printed “PIANO” on back and “13.” “K140” signifying that cabinet originally contained a JBL K140 piano or bass speaker for Phil Lesh. “Parish” referring to the band’s stage manager Steve Parish. On the top of the cabinet is the handwritten notation “Property of Simon Babbs & Tom Bassett.”  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.  Dimensions   Speaker cabinet: 19 ¼ x 16 ½ x 30 in.  Road case: 22 x 19 ¾ x 33 ½ in.

title: Grateful Dead
description_block: The itinerary was given to Bill Kelly, an insider of the band, after his hospitalization for injuries sustained in an attack. The itinerary features several personalized inscriptions to Kelly, wishing him health and a speedy recovery, including Jerry Garcia, who added "Watch it!!." Bill Kreutzmann wrote, “Billy, / This is kind of a gameball from everyone on the tour. I hope that you are up and about soon. Much love;" Phil Lesh added, humorously: “Dear Billy; Have a .45 installed in your cast and avoid high places / Phil.”

title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This cabinet was built for the Grateful Dead’s 1974 “Wall of Sound” and originally housed a speaker that carried Phil Lesh’s bass or for piano. In 1991, the cabinet was acquired by Simon Babbs, son of Ken Babbs who was a member of the Merry Pranksters and close collaborator of founder Ken Kesey. The cabinet was moved to Ken Kesey’s farm in Oregon where it was highly modified and painted red and white and then actively used by the Merry Pranksters Band. Photographs from early 1990s Fourth of July parties show the red Wall of Sound derived cabinets on the back of Kesey’s stage truck, with Ken and his wife Faye performing in front of them.  Cabinet has various stickers affixed including a “Free the Hostages,” dating back to the Iran Hostage Crisis which took place from 1979 to 1981; “Hard Truckers” circular sticker from the 1970s and 1980s. On the top of the cabinet is the handwritten notation “Property of Simon Babbs & Tom Bassett.”  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.  Dimensions   Speaker cabinet: 19 ¼ x 16 ½ x 30 in.  Road case: 22 x 19 ¾ x 33 ½ in.

title: B.B. King
description_block: The present guitar was played by B.B. King and used by him during the recording of B.B. King’s 1997 album  Deuces Wild , which featured a roster of all-star guitarists including Keith Richards, Jeff Beck, David Gilmour and Ron Wood.     This model is typical of the type of Gibson guitar that B.B. King played.

title: Elvis Presley
description_block: This Elvis-owned and signed bible was presented to the singer by a fan, who inscribed it to him, “This book will keep you from sin and only sin will keep you from this book. With love, Joy Woodson.” The bible ended up at Graceland and was given to recent owner by Elvis’ aunt, Delta Presley. Offered with letters of provenance from former owner and printed photographs of Delta Presley.

title: The Beatles
description_block: This drum was used in the 1996 video for “Real Love,” a song based on a John Lennon demo. Lennon’s original   demo was recorded in 1979 and 1980. In January 1994, Paul McCartney attended John Lennon's induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in New York. After the induction ceremony, McCartney met with Yoko Ono at the Dakota and she gave him two cassette tapes which included the “Real Love” demo. Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr overdubbed new, additional music and released the song as part of  The Beatles Anthology.  The drum is featured floating on-screen in the video.

title: John Lennon | Yoko Ono
description_block: “Sisters, O Sisters” was written by Yoko Ono in 1971, with the basic track development completed in February of 1972. The song was recorded on 28 February 28 1972, with this specific acetate being cut on the next day (29 February 1972) and lacking the final string overdubs.  The song first appeared on John and Yoko’s 1972 Plastic Ono Band album  Some Time in New York City,  backed by Elephant's Memory. “Sisters, O Sisters” was produced by Lennon and Phil Spector to include Spector’s atypical Wall of Sound girl group sound.

title: George Harrison | The Beatles
description_block: Acetates of  The Beatles: 1962–1966  and  The Beatles: 1967–1970  (also known as the “Red” and “Blue” albums). Four 12” discs with Apple Records Inc labels and typed track listings, in original 12 ½ x 12 ½ in. jackets.     These acetates were owned by George Harrison and later given to Chris O’Dell, who worked for Apple Records and was close friends with Harrison.  Includes signed letter from O’Dell: “This letter is to certify that the 2 sets of double albums, referred to as the Red and Blue albums, were given to me by George Harrison. He was in Los Angeles in 1973 and received these acetates from Capitol Records to listen to and approve.  When he was leaving to return to England he gave them to me.  I have never personally played these acetates nor has anyone else since they've been in my possession. I, therefore, assume only George played them. They have never been out of my possession since 1973.”

title: Bill Wyman
description_block: Bill Wyman’s subtle bass playing provided a distinctive and indelible impact on the Rolling Stones sound. Although his approach wasn’t flashy, when he locked in with drummer Charlie Watts, the Stones’ rhythm section became a iconic feature of the band’s sound.

There is no label on the “Silver Train” side of the acetate.  The disc exhibits light surface scratches; overall very good condition. Green and white label is slightly discolored. The sound quality of the recording on the disc is excellent with a slightly brighter mix, vibrant highs and strong bass, having been dubbed directly from the master tape recording.

title: Freddie Mercury
description_block: Munich was a deeply important place to Freddie Mercury, providing not only a temporary home but a level of respite from the public eye he simply could not get in London. Living there from 1979 until 1983, while his legendary Garden Lodge was under renovation, he deliberately immersed himself in the city’s nightlife and social scene. This t-shirt has direct ties to Mercury’s robust social life during his Munich years; it originates from the Münchner Löwen Club (Munich Lions Club), a gay leather and fetish club founded in 1974, which became one of Mercury’s haunts during his time in the city.

title: Sabrina Carpenter
description_block: Sabrina Carpenter wore the present outfit in the music video for “Because I Liked a Boy,” released in 2022 as a response to the surge of online backlash she faced following her alleged involvement in a love triangle with fellow Gen Z stars Olivia Rodrigo and Joshua Bassett. The narrative surrounding this supposed “love triangle” became the subject of intense social media discourse, intensified by fans’ efforts to interpret Rodrigo’s and Carpenter’s lyrics as veiled references to one another.

The sunglasses are made by one of his favorite brands which was Versace.”

Manufactured by Victor Shirts, Ibiza.  23 ½ in. pit-to-pit. 33 in. long. All measurements taken flat.

title: Pete Townshend
description_block: The guitar this fragment originates from was smashed by Pete Townshend on stage at The Who’s 19 November 1967 concert at Union Catholic High School in Scotch Plains, New Jersey.     Fan Bart Koster of Midtown Recording received the remains of the guitar from Townshend, noting: “Pete Townshend handed me the remains of the black Coral Hornet after smashing it at the Nov. 29, 1967, Scotch Plains Catholic High concert. What I have is about ¾ of the body of the guitar. I was 13 years old at the time. The back of my head can be seen in the lower left corner of two photos from that concert. I had the electronics initially, but gave those to my friend who fended off all the people that were trying to take it away from me. I recently found him after many years. As it turns out he lost those parts over time.”    Bob Pridden, the Who’s principal sound technician, told fans after the show that Pete had purchased several Coral Hornets on about 25 November 1967 from Manny’s Music in New York, when the group also purchased Sunn amplifiers and a Sunn PA. Pete Townshend used Coral Hornet guitars on stage in 1967 and 1968 and in his home studio until at least 1971.    Pete Townshend is famous for smashing his guitars during live performances. The destruction of an instrument was seen as an act of defiance and was especially shocking in the 1960s. Townshend’s repeated act of destroying his guitars was elevated to an act of performance art that audiences eventually anticipated and adored.

title: Keith Moon | The Who
description_block: A group of Keith Moon-related ephemera: a pair of Olympic C drumsticks, stage-used by Moon; a 7” paper plate signed on recto by Moon in blue ink (exhibiting creases throughout and browning on verso); an original concert ticket for the Who’s 2 November 1973 show at King’s Hall, Belle Vue in Manchester (right corner torn); and a black coiled amp cable (with frayed end). Offered with letter of provenance from original owner, who obtained these items directly from the band during their aforementioned Manchester show.

title: Led Zeppelin
description_block: "The Object" was designed by George Hardie and Hipgnosis, a design company that worked with many British acts. It supposedly represented the band's power and mystery.

title: Robert Plant | Jimmy Page
description_block: Jimmy Page pioneered the use of the double-neck guitar during live performances so he could quickly change from a 6-string to 12-string instrument mid-performance. He had a custom Gibson EDS-1275 double-neck made to his specifications, specifically to perform “Stairway to Heaven.” It immediately became an iconic guitar that other artists would emulate. The present Cozart guitar is patterned after the EDS-1275.

title: Led Zeppelin
description_block: 8 ½ x 5 ⅞ in. flyer, reinforced on cardstock, advertising Led Zeppelin’s shows at London’s Earl’s Court on 23, 24 and 25 May 1975. Signed in blue ballpoint by the band: Jimmy Page, Robert Plant, John Paul Jones, and John Bonham. Excellent condition.

title: The Sugarhill Gang
description_block: The track that brought hip-hop to the mainstream, “Rapper’s Delight” by the Sugarhill Gang is widely considered the first commercial rap song. Laid down in one nearly 15-minute take by three effectively amateur emcees, the song’s legacy is profound and ever-apparent. Constantly on rotation, the song received significant radio play—boosting record sales and breaking hip-hop from the confines of Bronx-born block parties to international airwaves. Despite the bassline and much of the lyrical content having been cribbed from other artists, the song was an unequivocal hit, peaking at number 36 on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 1980 and legitimizing rap as a genre worthy of recording. The song’s cultural significance was further affirmed when the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry in 2011, with an accompanying statement noting, “Although, it became famous on the back of serious claims of intellectual theft, ‘Rapper’s Delight’ has stood its ground and never crumbled over time. It is an invaluable requirement in the world of hip-hop, propelling rap music into what it is today.” While the song achieved near-instant commercial success, the Sugarhill Gang’s swift ascent marked a notable—and somewhat divisive—moment in the genre’s early development, as the group was assembled in northern New Jersey by producer Sylvia Robinson rather than authentically originating from the Bronx’s foundational scene. Still, many of the most notable hip-hop artists have cited “Rapper’s Delight” as having deep personal resonance, honoring the song for its groundbreaking achievements—including Queen Latifah, Chuck D, DJ Jazzy Jeff, Doug E. Fresh, and Method Man.

title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This birch-plywood speaker cabinet prototype was built in June 1972 at the Alembic shop by Rick Turner and Ron Wickersham labeled “COSMIC 672” in red; similar to other Alembic PA cabinets built for the Dead in 1972 and 1973. Cabinet also contained a JBL K140 Speaker for the piano that was converted into a bass cabinet for Phil Lesh with handprinted “Parish Side.” Steve Parish was stage manager for the 1974 Grateful Dead and a member of the band’s road crew.   This cabinet is one of Stanley “Bear’” Owsley’s first hifi creations that had individual Altec and JBL speakers for each instrument, driven by McIntosh power amps—and that debuted at the Cow Palace on March 23, 1974.  In practice, cabinets such as the “COSMIC 672” were the pieces the crew listened to, measured, and retuned as they worked out how to eliminate distortion, remove the need for stage monitors, and give each player a dedicated, full range PA of their own.  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.  Dimensions   Speaker cabinet: 30 ¾ x 15 x 14 ¾ in.  Road case: 34 ½ x 18 ½ x 16 ¼ in.

title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This birch plywood cabinet with JBL K120 and JBL 2202A loudspeakers, built specifically for keyboardist Keith Godchaux’s piano channel and engineered to capture the instantaneous, vertical hammerstrike of a grand piano. Cabinet was built in early 1974 by members of the Grateful Dead road crew—known in later years as Hard Truckers—in collaboration with the Alembic shop in San Francisco.   During the 1974 Wall of Sound tour in the United States, the cabinet was part of the dedicated piano cluster feeding Keith Godchaux’s grand piano. When the system was scaled and adapted for European dates later that year, piano and bass cabinets like this one traveled with the band.  “209” handwritten in marker on the back and right side, consistent with Wall of Sound box numbering practices. “PIANO” hand-stenciled in blue paint on the back toward the bottom (partially over sprayed with white paint), identifying this box as part of the piano array. On the JBL K120, the interior paper cone bears the signature “Kevin Konecky” in white marker. Konecky was a Wall of Sound audio engineer who worked closely with Owsley “Bear” Stanley on design, setup, and nightly operation. On the interior frame of the JBL 2202A, the name “Stereo Doctor” is written in white marker, echoing the nickname used for Owsley “Bear” Stanley in his capacity as the system’s chief sound architect. A period “Grim Reaper” violinist sticker appears on the right side of the cabinet. This image, designed by Alton Kelley, was used on Grateful Dead tour stickers circa 1973 and is frequently associated with the Dead’s own stage and road gear from that era.  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.  Dimensions   Speaker: 21 x 16 ½ x 26 in.  Road case: 25 ½ x 19 ¾ x 29 ½ in.

title: Grateful Dead
description_block: This birch plywood cabinet from the Grateful Dead’s “Wall of Sound” speaker system for Keith Godchaux’s acoustic piano. The cabinet features a pair of JBL D120F loudspeakers—high efficiency, 12 in. Alnico drivers codeveloped by JBL and Fender.   This cabinet was built in early 1974 by Alembic workers in conjunction with the Grateful Dead road crew—later known as Hard Truckers—in the San Francisco Bay Area. The materials, joinery, custom brackets, and removable baffle match other documented Wall of Sound boxes. It was numbered “208” and stenciled “PIANO,” marking it as part of Keith’s array.   Back of frame carries “G.D.” (Grateful Dead), “Ram…,” (Referring to the band’s roadie Laurence Shurtliff aka “Ramrod.” “Lumier,” “S.F.,” referring to the Lumiere Theatre and the date “32374,” the day the completed Wall of Sound debuted at the Cow Palace in Daly City, California.  On 23 March 1974, the fully realized “Wall of Sound” made its touring debut at the Cow Palace. The “32374” marking on one of the D120F frames aligns with that rollout. The piano cabinets—including No. 208—were used behind and above the band as part of the modular piano array, giving Keith Godchaux his channel. When the system was adapted for the European leg later that year, piano and bass cabinets like this one were part of the traveling inventory.

title: Grateful Dead
description_block: Phil Lesh Bass Cabinet with JBL D140F Loudspeaker with birch construction built in the San Francisco Bay Area by the Grateful Dead road crew (later known as Hard Truckers) in collaboration with Alembic. Assigned to Phil Lesh's bass array and matched to his famous Osiris bass guitar. Lesh debuted his Osiris bass on stage 16 June 1974, and he played it at nearly every show through 1979, including footage shot at Cornell University on 8 May 1977, the Great Pyramid concerts, and the closing of Winterland. This cabinet was purpose-built for that specific instrument.  Lesh's bass setup featured a custom quadraphonic, six channel instrument that sent each of its four strings to a separate channel. This cabinet was one of the dedicated low frequency boxes in that bass array.  A New Riders of the Purple Sage sticker on the cabinet side places its use in 1974, when the New Riders regularly opened for the Dead and shared access to the “Wall of Sound.”  With new custom road case decorated with stickers.  Dimensions   Speaker cabinet: 25 ¼ x 20 x 28 ½ in.   Road case: 29 x 23 ¾ x 32 ½ in.

title: Grateful Dead

Approximate weight: 240 lbs.

title: U2
description_block: The Joshua Tree , U2’s fifth album, sees the band pushing forward with tighter, more concise writing with the same impassioned plea. The romance of “With Or Without You,” the gospel of “I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For,” the Hendrix-like psychedelic on “Bullet The Blue Sky;” each showcase the band’s expanding range. Since its release, Joshua Tree is regarded as one of the great rock works of all time. The present item was signed by U2 in 1987 as part of a surprise signing session the night of the album’s release, hosted at Makin’ Tracks, a record store in Belfast, Ireland, that has since closed. Together with clipping of newspaper article about the event, as well as the original owner’s receipt and queue number ticket from said signing.

title: Noel Gallagher | Oasis
description_block: The song is the first Oasis single to feature Noel Gallagher singing lead vocals. Prior to that, he only sang lead on the group’s B-sides; his brother Liam Gallagher is the band’s main vocalist.    In 1995, Noel Gallagher told  Rolling Stone , "It's not about being upset about the things you might have said or done yesterday, which is quite appropriate at the moment. It's about looking forward rather than looking back. I hate people who look back on the past or talk about what might have been.”     The song’s title is a combination of D.A. Pennebaker's 1967 Bob Dylan documentary  Don’t Look Back  and the David Bowie song, "Look Back in Anger." The song also references English playwright and actor John Osborne's 1956 play Look Back in Anger .      In a 2019 interview with  Esquire , Noel Gallagher said, "I remember writing it in Paris on a rainy night. We had just played a strip club: our set finished; the strippers came on. We were nothing, an insignificant little band. And I remember going back to my hotel room and writing it, and thinking, 'That'll be pretty good when we record it.' If I'd have known that night what I know now about people playing it at f***ing funerals and weddings, I'd never have finished the song. Too much pressure."

title: Noel Gallagher | Oasis
description_block: Oasis’ sophomore project (What’s The Story) Morning Glory?  essentially became a greatest hits album, including the songs: “Champagne Supernova,” “Morning Glory,” “Wonderwall,” “Roll with It,” “Don’t Look Back in Anger,” “Some Might Say” and others. A smash hit that would come to define an entire musical movement, it is arguably the most distinct and iconic release of the band’s discography—and the present guitar, Noel Gallagher’s Epiphone EJ-200, played a role in its creation. One of the crown jewels of Britpop, Morning Glory catapulted Oasis into international megastardom—a supernova in their own right. Gallagher’s songwriting on the album—some of which took place using the present instrument—is both nostalgic and forward-looking, a microcosm of the band’s eminence across time. A testament to their enduring influence and cross-generational appeal, the band has enjoyed quite the renaissance in the present cultural zeitgeist. On the heels of the Gallagher brothers’ long-awaited reconciliation, Oasis embarked on a wildly successful reunion tour in 2025—finding a new audience among Gen Z while giving their longtime, diehard fanbase the chance to reminisce on all the moments and memories that inspired their love of the band in the first place.

title: The Beatles
description_block: The Beatles' live performances at the Star-Club in Hamburg in late 1962 are legendary for giving them space to hone their sound just before their global breakthrough. While Pete Best was the drummer for their earliest Hamburg stints, Ringo Starr had officially joined by their final residency in December 1962, providing the steady, driving backbeat that defined their polished yet raw live energy.

title: The Beatles
description_block: After a three month break from the recording studios and a trip to India where most of the new material was written, The Beatles were back at EMI Studios to start the recording of their new album, which would officially be named “The Beatles” and unofficially—though more commonly—called the "White Album.” A double album with over 30 new songs, the album was recorded between 30 May and 14 October 1968, largely at Abbey Road Studios in London.

title: Plastic Ono Band | John Lennon and Yoko Ono
description_block: 12 x 12 in. album, catalogue number SVBB 3392, manufactured by Apple Records. Signed by John Lennon and Yoko Ono in black felt tip pen on front cover. Together with two LPs and accompanying inserts.

title: John Lennon
description_block: This intimate group of materials offers a rare and deeply personal insight into John Lennon’s intellectual curiosity, artistic spontaneity, and cultural engagement during a formative period in the artist’s life and relationship with Yoko Ono. In 1976, Lennon enrolled in a Berlitz “Total Immersion” Japanese language crash course to prepare for an upcoming extended trip to Japan, where he would spend time with Yoko’s family. Conducted entirely in Japanese, the program followed a rigorous, intensive curriculum, with full days devoted to language instruction both inside and beyond the classroom.  Course materials included illustrated booklets designed to facilitate vocabulary acquisition and retention; Lennon, characteristically, transformed his own booklet into a site of playful creative expression, embellishing the prescribed imagery with spontaneous and simple—yet quite meaningful—doodles. As he continued in his studies, he incorporated a sketchbook, reportedly gifted during his first week of the course, in which he visually recorded newly-acquired words and phrases in his signature line-drawing style. These doodles, often infused with his irreverent humor and a touch of whimsy, reveal a deeper impression of Lennon’s imagination and his innate ability to create meaning in the mundane.  To "Steinberg san," according to her daughter, Lennon was remembered as an exceptionally fast and intuitive learner—the “fastest natural learner” she had worked with, which prompted her to wonder whether his “genius with music” is what made him so well-equipped as a pupil. A postcard sent from Japan, included in this lot, later affirmed his progress, noting that he had received compliments on his spoken Japanese. This personal yet playful peek into John Lennon’s academic life is evidence of a deeper relationship between student and teacher: one of mutual admiration, respect, and boundless creativity. In these items, it is clear that Lennon found immense fulfillment from his studies, and that his time in the course served him well during his travels to Japan.   Lennon’s connection to Japan extended well beyond this period of formal language study, becoming a focal point of his personal and artistic life in the later years of his career. Through his relationship with Yoko Ono, Lennon developed a sustained interest in Japanese culture, aesthetics and, clearly, language. Japan became a much-needed refuge, culturally and creatively, for Lennon—particularly during his “househusband” years in the late 1970s, during which he focused on the tranquility of domestic life. He spent some summers during this period in Karuizawa, a serene mountain resort town near Nagano.

title: Paul McCartney
description_block: The Höfner bass guitar, with its iconic violin-shaped body, served as Paul McCartney’s primary instrument and can be heard on the vast majority of The Beatles’ recordings. Its hollow-body construction produces a distinctive, warm, and resonant tone with a subtle acoustic quality.

title: Ravi Shankar
description_block: 29 booklets of Ravi Shankar’s score for the Concerto for Sitar and Orchestra—14 for Violin 1, 13 for Violin 2, one for Bass, and one for Horns 1 & 2—with annotations in pencil throughout, as well as four ragas handwritten in ballpoint: Marwa, Yaman, Nata [sic] Bhairav, and Bhimpalasi. Together with two invoice sheets on Tatra Corporation letterhead, one blank and one addressed to the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra.

title: George Harrison | Ravi Shankar
description_block: In 1971, sitarist Ravi Shankar informed George Harrison about the humanitarian crisis in Bangladesh, which was known as East Pakistan at the time. Harrison immediately approached many of his friends and fellow musicians to play two charity concerts to benefit the people of East Pakistan, collectively titled the Concert for Bangladesh. Held at Madison Square Garden on 1 August 1971, there was a matinee and evening performance.  Ringo Starr appeared with Harrison—marking the first time since 1966 that the two had appeared together in a live performance. Eric Clapton, Bob Dylan, Ravi Shankar and Billy Preston also performed, among others. The corresponding triple album was produced by Phil Spector. The Concert for Bangladesh was the first staged concert of rock superstars, a trend that later became ubiquitous.

title: Pink Floyd
description_block: In Pink Floyd’s early incarnation, when the group was led by Syd Barrett, their sound was psychedelic. They were recording at Abbey Road upstairs when the Beatles were also working in the building. Games for May, one of the first significant live events held by the band, was described as a “space age relaxation for the climax of spring - electronic composition, color and image projection, girls and the Pink Floyd.” The concert featured some of the band's early singles as well as material from their yet to be released debut album, The Piper at the Gates of Dawn .

title: Richard Wright
description_block: Letter from Franka Wright states: “This guitar is part [sic] of my memorys [sic] is Ricks [sic] (Ricardos [sic]) guitar.” Letter also discusses Wright relaxing with the guitar at home on a boat in Greece.     Wright co-founded Pink Floyd and played on nearly every one of the band’s albums. He performed on every Pink Floyd tour and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of Floyd in 1996.

title: David Bowie
description_block: “The Jean Genie” was released as a single in November 1972 and included in the 1973 album Aladdin Sane . The lyrics were inspired by Cyrinda Foxe, an actress and model who was part of Andy Warhol’s circle. In fact, Bowie began writing the tune with the hopes of wooing Foxe. Bowie recalled, “Starting out as a lightweight riff thing I had written one evening in New York for Cyrinda’s enjoyment. I developed the lyric to the otherwise wordless pumper and it ultimately turned into a bit of a smorgasbord of imagined Americana... based on an Iggy-type persona," the artist shared in book Moonage Daydream. "The title, of course, was a clumsy pun upon Jean Genet." The song was recorded in New York City’s RCA Studios on 6 October 1972.

title: Madonna
description_block: Custom cranberry red wool felt fedora, measuring 5 in. tall, with 21 ¼ in. circumference and 2 ¾ in. brim. Together with 5 x 6 ⅝ in. photograph of Madonna wearing fedora and original black custom hat box. Hat box is 6 in. tall, with 13 in. diameter. Offered with Letter of Authenticity and Letter of Provenance from current consignor.

title: Stevie Nicks
description_block: Black velvet jacket with dramatic collar, signed on synthetic lining by Stevie Nicks in silver ink. Label, no tags or closures. Seams loose/unattached at hem.  Jacket is 24 in. pit-to-pit, 16 in. shoulder-to-shoulder, 9 in. sleeve, 40 in. long, with 9 in. tall collar. All measurements taken flat. Offered with certificate of authenticity from Funtyme Memorabilia.

title: Stevie Nicks
description_block: A 9” tambourine played by Stevie Nicks live on stage and inscribed in black marker, “Much love Stevie Nicks enjoy!” Mounted in 21 ⅜ x 35 ¼ x 3 in. frame with a black and white photograph of Stevie Nicks signed in gold paint pen, “Much love Stevie Nicks.” Stevie Nicks plays tambourine when performing live and the instrument is an integral part of her stage persona.

title: Stevie Nicks
description_block: A black felt top hat with red fabric band and silver encrusted moon-and-star brooch, signed by Stevie Nicks in gold ink. The hat is 6 ¼ in. tall, with a 21 ½ in. circumference and a 2 ¼ in. brim. Offered with JSA Letter of Authenticity.

title: Joni Mitchell
description_block: With “Marcie,” Joni Mitchell offers a poignant vignette of a forlorn woman waiting in vain for a lover who never returns. Vivid imagery of changing seasons underscore Marcie’s loss of hope; as the green of summer fades into an autumnal red—and, eventually, a wind-chilled winter—so too does Marcie’s hope that her sorrows may one day be answered by the man she so dearly longs for. Characteristically Mitchell, the song powerfully grapples with themes of love, loss, and longing.  A wistful, evocative ballad, “Marcie” is but one example of Mitchell’s sheer talent as a songwriter and storyteller; Song to a Seagull is replete with Mitchell’s exceptional ability to paint rich pictures with her lyrics—a true wordsmith at work.

title: Jimmy Buffett
description_block: 11 x 14 ⅛ in. 2 pp. manuscript in black pen on unruled white notebook paper, being a working draft of Jimmy Buffett’s “The Good Fight.” Lyrics on recto and verso; verso also contains guitar chords.

title: Bruce Springsteen
description_block: 12 x 12 in. Born in the U.S.A. album, signed on the front cover by Springsteen in blue marker. Together with LP and accompanying inserts.

title: Bruce Springsteen
description_block: 8 ⅜ x 11 in. 1p. Manuscript, written by Bruce Springsteen in pencil on lined notebook paper. features developmental draft of “Backstreets,” with several lines from the finished work, including: “Just another tramp of hearts crying tears of faithlessness…. Stranded in the park and forced to confess.”    Released on Bruce Springsteen's 1975 masterwork,  Born to Run , “Backstreets” is evocative of Bob Dylan’s “Positively 4th Street,” particularly in the melody and organ, which bear a strong resemblance to the Dylan song.

title: Neil Young
description_block: The grey corduroy jacket, khaki pants and white dress shirt by Gentleman Farmer worn by Neil Young during the Continental tour. During the tour, Young commissioned painter Eric Johnson to create artwork live on stage during the shows. These paintings, produced during the concerts, often resulted in paint stains on Young’s clothing during his interaction with the artwork—clearly visible on the present suit. Blazer: 22 in. pit-to-pit, 32 ½ in. long, 25 ½ in. sleeve, 20 in. shoulder-to-shoulder Shirt: 24 in. pit-to-pit, 30 ¾ in. long, 25 ½ in. sleeve, 19 in. shoulder-to-shoulder Pants: 16 ½ in. waist, 32 in. inseam, 42 in. leg All measurements taken flat.

title: Bob Dylan
description_block: 12 x 12 in. Blonde on Blonde album, signed on the front cover by Bob Dylan in black felt tip pen. Includes both records.  Offered with letter of provenance from Jeff Rosen, Dylan’s manager.

title: Bob Dylan
description_block: A Martin Smith W-101-N-PK acoustic guitar, autographed on body by Bob Dylan in black marker, Joan Baez in silver marker, Eric Andersen in red marker, and Charlie Sexton in silver marker. Dylan has added “Best wishes;” Baez has added “To Dino / love Joan Baez;” Andersen has added “5/13/22 / Italy” to mark the date of his corresponding Bob Dylan tribute concert in Parma on that day. Excellent condition. Dimensions Guitar: 40 ½ x 14 ⅝ x 4 ¼ in.

title: Bob Dylan
description_block: This poster advertises Bob Dylan’s "Only New York Concert Appearance" on 31 October 1964—both Saturday night and Halloween. Dylan was in a great mood and was particularly funny that evening, even joking from the stage, “It's Halloween and I've got my Bob Dylan mask on." The audience was enraptured.     It was an especially memorable performance—regarded as one of if not the best acoustic shows of Dylan’s career. Joan Baez came on stage and joined him for several songs.    Dylan performed the yet to be released "Mr. Tambourine Man.” Other songs performed include "The Times They Are A-Changin'," "It's Alright, Ma (I'm Only Bleeding)," "A Hard Rain's A-Gonna Fall," "Don't Think Twice, It's All Right," "It Ain't Me Babe," and "All I Really Want to Do." Columbia Records released the concert as part of  The Bootleg Series.

title: Bob Dylan
description_block: 12 x 12 in. Hearts of Fire (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack) album, inscribed “London Rocks!!” and signed on the front cover by Bob Dylan, Rupert Everett, and Fiona (Flanagan) in silver marker.

title: Bob Dylan
description_block: During this show, Dylan played sets of both folk music and electric rock ‘n’ roll. The electric set was booed by the hardcore folkies who couldn’t get over that Dylan was rewriting the rules yet again, expanding his sound with electric rock and roll.    His backing group for the electric set featured Robbie Robertson on electric guitar, Rick Danko on bass, Richard Manuel on piano, and Garth Hudson on organ.

title: Stevie Wonder
description_block: A Hohner Special 20 harmonica in key of F, signed by Stevie Wonder in black marker. Together with a Hohner-branded gray plastic case, also signed by Stevie Wonder in gold marker. Offered with JSA Letter of Authenticity.

title: Lady Gaga
description_block: The present shirt was worn by Lady Gaga during Carpool Karaoke’s first ever Christmas special in December 2024. The special also featured Dua Lipa and Chappell Roan, and was guest hosted by radio personality and television presenter Zane Lowe.

title: Olivia Rodrigo
description_block: The present garment appeared on the cover of Music Week ’s December 2021 issue, in which she was also named the magazine’s 2021 Artist Of The Year.  Regarding the honor, and Rodrigo’s then-nascent power as an artist, Polydor Records president Ben Mortimer noted, “I think we’d all be lying if we said we knew the extent of what was coming with Olivia. Her being named Artist Of The Year is amazing. It’s great and I think she deserves it. We had inklings of a new signing Interscope were really excited about before Christmas in 2020. Then when we came back after Christmas the world of Olivia had gone completely mad. It became apparent, very quickly, that they had signed a wonderful artist who was riding on the wave of a cultural phenomenon.”

title: Prince
description_block: Black soft leather jacket, worn by Prince on the cover of his career-defining 1986 single "Kiss," bedazzled in geometric patterns with rhinestones throughout. In very good vintage condition, with oversized fit. Zipper closure working; all rhinestones in place; cinching effect at waist removed for baggier fit; loose threads at seams; small stain on back collar. 18 ½ in. shoulder-to-shoulder, 26 in. pit-to-pit; 14 in. sleeve, 21 in. waist, 31 in. long. All measurements taken flat.

title: Prince
description_block: 28 x 21 ⅞ in. Poster of Prince and his band, The Revolution, from the Purple Rain LP, signed by Prince in black ink and inscribed, “Love God.”

title: Prince
description_block: 8 ½ x 10 in. 1 p. manuscript in pencil on ruled notebook paper, being a near-final version of “3121,” the opening track of Prince’s 2006 album of the same name.  Features the song’s chorus, three verses, outro, and an alternative version of the intro. Prince uses shorthand (e.g. “u” to represent “you;” “c” to represent “see;” “ur” to represent “your”) throughout.  Offered with JSA Letter of Authenticity.

title: Taylor Swift
description_block: 12 x 12 in. 1989 album cover, signed by Taylor Swift in black marker.

title: Michael Jackson | The Jackson 5
description_block: Red polo shirt with gray buttons at collar. Features blue embroidered music note and “J5” detail at left chest. No labels or interior tags. Visible mend at collar, snags throughout.  21 in. long, 15 in. shoulder-to-shoulder, 15 in. pit-to-pit, 12 in. waist. All measurements taken flat. Letter of provenance signed by Michael Jackson’s assistant Frank Cascio, who received the shirt as a gift from Jackson.

title: Jimi Hendrix
description_block: 7 ⅛ x 7 in. Sleeve for Jimi Hendrix’s “Purple Haze,” signed by Hendrix on recto in black marker. Small piece of black tape affixed around top left corner of recto. Sleeve exhibits cracking along edges and slightly bumped corners. Signature and album artwork intact on both sides.

title: Janis Joplin
description_block: This show at New York City's Madison Square Garden was Joplin’s last performance with her backing group, The Kosmic Blues Band. The concert featured the Paul Butterfield Blues Band as the opening act. Guitarist and singer Johnny Winter also made an appearance.
